query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges when the initially fine, nano-sized Mn₂O₃ precipitates (formed during rapid solidification via SLM) coarsen or become interconnected at cell/grain boundaries – for example, via controlled oxygen enrichment or thermal aging – thereby creating local stress concentrations that weaken grain boundary cohesion and reduce ductility. This mechanism is distinct from conventional alloys where grain-boundary segregation of solute atoms predominates.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase CoCrFeMnNi HEA produced by selective laser melting, featuring a fine distribution (≈27 nm) of Mn₂O₃ precipitates at cell or grain boundaries with high ductility and toughness under baseline testing conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled increase in oxygen content (or impose post-process thermal aging) to promote coarsening and potential interconnection of the Mn₂O₃ precipitates.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile and fracture toughness tests) under service-relevant loading rates and temperatures (from room temperature up to about 700 °C) in a controlled atmosphere to isolate the effect of oxygen, ensuring that all other processing parameters remain constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The size, spatial distribution, and connectivity of Mn₂O₃ precipitates at cell/grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under enhanced oxygen conditions or thermal aging, the nano-precipitates coarsen and may link up at boundaries. This transition reduces the beneficial Zener pinning effect and instead creates sites for stress concentration that promote localized intergranular fracture, leading to a transition from ductile to brittle failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens subjected to the oxygen-enhancing intervention are expected to show a measurable degradation in toughness and ductility relative to the baseline, with fracture surfaces exhibiting features consistent with intergranular or brittle fracture rather than the ductile features observed in the as-fabricated state.
generation.baseline: The as-produced HEA with uniformly fine Mn₂O₃ precipitates exhibiting high strength and ductility without significant brittle failure under comparable testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under typical service temperatures (up to about 700 °C) and steady loading rates; at much higher temperatures or under extreme strain rates, other deformation or failure mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical precipitate size or oxygen concentration threshold that triggers the brittle transition is not yet defined and requires further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi HEA specimens via SLM: one as a baseline with controlled low oxygen levels and one with an elevated oxygen content (or subjected to post-deposition thermal aging) to promote Mn₂O₃ precipitate coarsening. Perform identical mechanical tests (e.g., tensile, fracture toughness) over a range of temperatures (room temperature to 700 °C) while characterizing microstructural changes via TEM and SEM.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of precipitate size and distribution from TEM/SEM
Fracture surface analysis via SEM to determine brittle vs ductile features
Mechanical property measurements (toughness, ductility, stress-strain response)
Grain boundary chemistry analysis via EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-enriched/aged specimens do not demonstrate a significant coarsening of Mn₂O₃ precipitates or if there is no observable decrease in toughness and ductility (i.e., fracture behavior remains similar to the baseline), then the hypothesis that precipitate coarsening at boundaries drives brittle behavior is falsified.

System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used..
